We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.

[714] arXiv:2610.31671 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Unified Framework for Image-to-3D Part Generation via Variable Granularity
Qiwen Gu, Xin Zhou, Xiwu Chen, Zhongyang Zhu, Zhuo Zhang, Junqiao Zhao
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Controllable 3D part generation is pivotal for digital asset creation, yet existing methods lack the flexibility to accommodate diverse user workflows requiring varying levels of control. In this paper, we introduce FlexPart, a unified image-to-3D part generation framework that supports variable-granularity geometric conditions within a single model. By seamlessly integrating heterogeneous inputs, ranging from sparse points to dense bounding boxes and masks, via gated adaptive modulation, FlexPart unlocks a powerful cross-modal synergy. We also propose an asymmetric geometric guidance mechanism that leverages strong spatial priors to align representations across granularities, improving geometric consistency and facilitating inter-task synergy. Under mask conditioning on PartVerseXL, FlexPart reduces Part CD by 16.6% relative to TripoSG + SAM3D and by 10.5% relative to OmniPart, while maintaining competitive whole-mesh quality. The code can be found at this https URL

Cross submissions (showing 55 of 55 entries)

[715] arXiv:0905.4950 (cross-list from physics.bio-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
Chen Li, Paul B. Umbanhowar, Haldun Komsuoglu, Daniel E. Koditschek, Daniel I. Goldman
Journal-ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2009), 106 (9), 3029-3034
Subjects: Biological Physics (physics.bio-ph); Other Condensed Matter (cond-mat.other); Soft Condensed Matter (cond-mat.soft); Robotics (cs.RO); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)

Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $\phi$ and the limb frequency $\omega$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $\phi$ becomes small enough and/or $\omega$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.

[716] arXiv:2610.30141 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Consensus-Aware Co-design of Wireless Multi-Agent Control and Communication Systems
Atefeh Termehchi, Sajedeh Soleimani, Shiva Kazemi Taskooh, Mehdi Rasti, Ekram Hossain
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)

Autonomous multi-agent control systems (MACSs) enable distributed coordination in emerging applications such as smart power grids and autonomous vehicle or drone networks. In many of these applications, inter-agent communication relies on wireless networks. However, conventional MACS designs neglect the interaction between the communication and control subsystems. At the same time, conventional wireless designs reserve communication resources based on worst-case MACS requirements. Consequently, control performance is degraded and wireless resources are utilized inefficiently. To address these challenges, we propose a consensus-aware co-design approach for MACSs and wireless communication systems. We introduce a system model in which agents achieve consensus by exchanging information through device-to-device (D2D) links that share spectrum with cellular users under limited bandwidth resources. Based on this model, we formulate a joint optimization problem for consensus-topology selection and wireless resource allocation to minimize bandwidth consumption while guaranteeing consensus and satisfying the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of both MACSs and cellular users. Although the resulting problem is a mixed-integer nonlinear program (NP-hard in general), a structural property of the optimal solution enables a sequential two-stage optimization algorithm with polynomial complexity. Simulations on a smart power grid case study demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves 24-27% bandwidth savings compared with the two baselines while maintaining consensus and satisfying all QoS requirements of the control agents and the communication users.

[717] arXiv:2610.30148 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, other]
Title: Do Machine Learning-Guided Proactive Full Capacity Protocols Mitigate Emergency Department Overcrowding? A Simulation-Based Evaluation
Khalid Aram, Orhun Vural, Bunyamin Ozaydin, James Booth, Abdulaziz Ahmed
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Computers and Society (cs.CY); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Objective: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding threatens care quality, yet Full Capacity Protocols (FCPs) are typically activated only after crowding thresholds have been exceeded. This study evaluated whether machine learning-guided proactive FCP activation improves ED crowding control compared with conventional reactive activation.
Materials and Methods: We developed and validated an integrated machine learning and discrete-event simulation framework representing ED patient flow and capacity management. An embedded machine learning model predicted hourly waiting-room crowding six hours ahead and triggered proactive FCP activation. Using empirically calibrated operational parameters from a large US hospital, we compared proactive and reactive deployment strategies over a 365-day simulation horizon with 10 independent replications. Outcomes included ED length of stay, wait time, percentage of time above the crowding threshold, number of FCP activations, and protocol duration.
Results: Proactive deployment produced statistically significant reductions in the percentage of time above the crowding threshold and average protocol duration across all threshold settings. It also reduced crowding variability and extreme congestion events, resulting in smoother ED operations. Although proactive deployment generally improved ED length of stay and wait time, these differences were not statistically significant.
Conclusion: Embedding machine learning predictions within an operational simulation enables proactive, prediction-guided capacity management before severe congestion develops. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of proactive FCP deployment as a decision-support strategy for improving ED crowding control and provide evidence to support prospective implementation in clinical practice.

[718] arXiv:2610.30149 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Tutte-Like Theorem for Injective Flows on Meshes
Darsh Kaushik, Noam Aigerman
Comments: 12 pages, 11 figures
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Graphics (cs.GR)

This work proves a theorem regarding injectivity of continuous flows that are defined via discrete vector fields on triangle meshes. In similar fashion to Tutte's embedding, the theorem shows a connection between harmonicity and injectivity. Specifically, a discrete harmonic function is computed over a spherical mesh, and its $90^\circ$-rotated gradients are taken as the vector field. We show that this leads to an injective flow over the mesh, i.e., when two points are advected along the vector field, their trajectories are guaranteed to not intersect. The core insight behind this theorem is that the characterization of the Poincaré-Hopf indices of discrete harmonic 1-forms is paralleled in the combinatorial rules for injective vector fields. Similarly to Tutte's embedding, the injective vector field can be computed by simply solving a sparse linear system. Furthermore, it is differentiably dependent on the entries of the Laplacian, enabling unconstrained gradient-based optimization of the vector field while preserving injectivity. The advection itself can be computed by a quick and accurate algorithm. We experimentally validate the injectivity of the results, as well as show examples of differentiable optimization, such as computing an injective approximation to a given non-injective vector field, and fitting an injective vector field to satisfy constraints.

[719] arXiv:2610.30179 (cross-list from physics.flu-dyn) [pdf, html, other]
Title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction
Yatin Kumar, Shivani Saini, Ramesh Kumar Vats
Subjects: Fluid Dynamics (physics.flu-dyn); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Scientific machine learning provides a promising framework for solving complex problems in science and engineering. Notably, physics informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown considerable potential for solving differential equations and modelling engineering systems. Solving time fractional Navier Stokes equations (TFNSEs) on complex domains is challenging due to temporal nonlocality, nonlinear flow dynamics, geometric complexity, and incompressibility constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry gated, divergence-free Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov Arnold network (GeoDiv KAN). The proposed architecture uses geometry dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation to preserve incompressibility by construction. GeoDiv KAN is evaluated for the time fractional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on square, circular, and star-shaped domains. Numerical experiments show that GeoDiv KAN achieves higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN across the considered benchmark problems. To establish practical relevance, GeoDiv KAN is applied to two data driven CFD cases: unsteady flow past a circular cylinder using the \href{this https URL}{Zenodo dataset} and turbulent RANS flow through a complex U bend using the \href{this https URL}{U-bend dataset}.

[720] arXiv:2610.30186 (cross-list from astro-ph.IM) [pdf, html, other]
Title: SIGNN++: Robust Graph Neural Star Identification on Earth
Jeongbin Sohn, Jina Lee, Max Yen, Dowan Gwon, Jeahn Han, Floyd Hepburn-Dickins, Brian Coltin, Ryan Soussan, Pyojin Kim
Comments: 9 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables
Subjects: Instrumentation and Methods for Astrophysics (astro-ph.IM); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We present SIGNN++, a learning-based star identification (SID) framework for celestial navigation in GNSS-denied nighttime environments. Although researchers have developed learning-based SID methods to improve robustness to observation noise, prior evaluations have focused mainly on synthetic or non-terrestrial environments, leaving their reliability under real terrestrial conditions unclear. To address these limitations, SIGNN++ extends SIGNN, a graph neural network-based SID method, with three components: a more realistic noise model for training data, Fourier Transform (FT) of angular-distance edge features, and RANSAC-based Perspective Star Alignment for identification and attitude refinement. The results show that SIGNN++ is more robust to terrestrial observation disturbances and achieves higher star identification accuracy and solved rates than the original SIGNN and publicly available SID baselines, while maintaining comparable attitude accuracy and practical computation time for continuous operation. The implementation code of SIGNN++ and datasets will be available at this https URL.

[721] arXiv:2610.30191 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Why Constrained Updates Still Forget: A Functional-Path Analysis of Continual SFT
Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Supervised fine-tuning adapts language models to specialized tasks but can disrupt previously acquired behavior. Existing approaches constrain parameters, gradients, or replay objectives, yet the connection between the protected object, the intervening trajectory, and retained outputs remains unclear. We develop a functional-path account that decomposes old-loss changes along realized updates into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects. The account yields a conditional refresh budget and identifies the restoring direction supplied by informative replay. Matched QLoRA interventions separate constraint granularity from placement before or after Adam: placement strongly affects retention across the studied code-label audits, whereas the granularity interaction depends on the endpoint. Checkpointed generation separates endpoint recovery from higher sampled-path accuracy, and matched replay schedules reveal loss exposure concealed by final scores. A sequential-task comparison extends this distinction to backward transfer: subspace regularization and projection improve average retention while trading off different old tasks; supervised replay protects both more consistently in this setting. Additional response interfaces distinguish content gains from exact-response retention. These findings connect update-level protection to task-wise behavior and motivate mitigation through explicit functional anchors, trajectory evaluation, and joint old/new auditing.

[722] arXiv:2610.30196 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via Generalized Moment Matching
Rundong Ding, Yiyun He, Yizhe Zhu
Comments: 53 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Information Theory (cs.IT); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Probability (math.PR); Statistics Theory (math.ST)

We study $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private synthetic data for arbitrary databases of $n$ records in $[-1,1]^d$ under a specified integral probability metric (IPM). We introduce generalized moment matching, which estimates moments privately, fits a probability measure, and samples synthetic records. A general error theorem applies when moment error controls the target IPM. This framework extends Chebyshev moment matching for $1$-Wasserstein distance and smooth queries. We apply the framework to maximum mean discrepancy with Matern and Laplace kernels and a two-layer ReLU neural tangent this http URL also obtain guarantees for sliced Wasserstein-$1$ and the IPM induced by norm-bounded ReLU networks. With sufficiently many synthetic records,these rates are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed dimension.

[723] arXiv:2610.30313 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: SciFusion: Physics-Guided Compositional Diffusion for Multimodal 3D Scientific Image Generation
Luoxi Wang, Alessio Quercia, Hanno Scharr, Arya Bangun
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Existing 3D generative approaches are typically developed for individual imaging modalities, requiring substantial modality-specific data and limiting their ability to exploit shared structure across scientific imaging domains. We present SciFusion, a multimodal framework for unified 3D scientific image generation built on a latent diffusion backbone, with two key contributions. First, we introduce a compositional conditioning scheme that factorizes each modality into domain, object, and contrast representations. Sharing these factors across related modalities enables knowledge transfer across heterogeneous imaging domains and allows the factors to be recombined at inference time to synthesize unseen domain-object-contrast compositions in a zero-shot manner. Second, we incorporate domain-specific physics-informed objectives: Fourier spectral consistency for MRI, Radon projection consistency for CT, and multislice diffraction consistency for electron microscopy, to encourage generated samples to respect modality-dependent image formation processes. Extensive experiments across 15 medical and scientific imaging modalities demonstrate that SciFusion improves generation fidelity and cross-domain generalization over modality-specific and flattened multimodal conditioning strategies, while enabling zero-shot synthesis of unseen compositions without training on those target compositions. These results demonstrate that compositional, physics-guided conditioning provides a scalable framework for unified 3D scientific image generation, particularly for emerging modalities where large-scale training data are difficult to obtain.

[724] arXiv:2610.30388 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
Qian Zhang, Shanqing Liu, Jerome Darbon, George Karniadakis
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.

[725] arXiv:2610.30408 (cross-list from econ.TH) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Limits of Price Discrimination When the Market Is Unknown
Irfan Tekdir
Comments: 14 pages, 3 figures
Subjects: Theoretical Economics (econ.TH); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

Bergemann, Brooks, and Morris (2015) characterize the consumer and producer surplus pairs that segmentation can produce when the distribution of values is known. I fix only the set of possible values and characterize the pairs that some market and some segmentation can produce. They form a convex polygon. Its outer edge is the largest efficient surplus a market can have when its uniform-price profit is capped, net of that profit, and truncated equal-revenue markets attain it. At the values no segmentation is needed; strictly between two values, reaching the frontier requires splitting a market into two extremal markets. With a continuum of values up to $\bar{v}$, consumer surplus is at most $\pi\ln(\bar{v}/\pi)$ when producer surplus (the seller's profit) is $\pi$, this bound is reached without segmentation, and no market gives consumers more than $\bar{v}/e$.

[726] arXiv:2610.30421 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: High-Value Training Data from Noisy, Diverse Sources
Hedi Driss, Evan Frick, Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Cho-Jui Hsieh, Yejin Huh, Tijana Zrnic, Andrew Ilyas
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Training state-of-the-art models increasingly requires learning from large, heterogeneous datasets whose examples vary in quality, domain relevance, and source of supervision. Dataweighting---assigning different weights to training examples---offers a general way to control how such data influences training, but learning effective weights at scale remains challenging. We develop a scalable approach to learning dataweights: given a small, high-quality target dataset, we use metagradients through the training process to efficiently optimize training-example weights directly for performance on the target domain. To scale beyond a fixed dataset and model, we learn parametric weighting rules that generalize to new and streaming examples and transfer from smaller models to substantially larger ones. We study reward modeling as a prototypical application, where preference data may be noisy, adversarial, synthetic, or mismatched with the target domain. Learned dataweights improve held-out performance, automatically adapt reward models to specialized domains, and allow mixtures of human and synthetic supervision to outperform either source alone.

[727] arXiv:2610.30465 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
Zi Yang, Ying Li, Alejandro Lancho, Darío C. Larese, Pablo M. Olmos, Michael Minyi Zhang
Comments: 23 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: this https URL.

[728] arXiv:2610.30562 (cross-list from stat.ME) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
Xiaojing Sun, Yuhan Zeng, Xiao Wang
Subjects: Methodology (stat.ME); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.

[729] arXiv:2610.30615 (cross-list from math.CO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Ternary and Quaternary Cases of the $\{2,4\}$-Distance Code Conjecture
Yen-Chi Roger Lin, Valjakas Djaljapayan, Wei-Hsuan Yu
Subjects: Combinatorics (math.CO); Information Theory (cs.IT)

For an integer $q\ge2$, let $A_q(n,\{2,4\})$ be the largest cardinality of an unrestricted $q$-ary code of length $n$ in which any two distinct words have Hamming distance $2$ or $4$. We prove that \[
A_q(n,\{2,4\})=1+\binom n2
\qquad(q\in\{3,4\},\ n\ge6), \] thereby settling the two remaining alphabet sizes in the conjecture of Boyvalenkov, Delchev, Zinoviev, and Zinoviev; the binary case was settled previously. The quaternary result implies the ternary result by alphabet inclusion. For $n\ge16$, the quaternary upper bound is proved combinatorially. After normalizing one word to zero, the weight-four supports form a $2$-intersecting family; exact support intersections force symbol synchronization and restrict support multiplicities. We combine the nontrivial intersection theorem with matching arguments and a three-coordinate projection lemma. The finite lengths $6\le n\le13$ are handled by a complete Hamming-isometry reduction to exact clique decisions, and $n=14,15$ by a smaller exact weighted-clique relaxation. All finite decisions are reproduced by two standalone integer-only C++17 verifiers provided as supplementary source files.

[730] arXiv:2610.30616 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: On the Structure of Quantum Finite-Level Systems: Decoherence-Free Subsystems, Quantum Nondemolition Variables, and Back-Action-Evading Measurements
Jia Gu, Guofeng Zhang, Ian R. Petersen
Comments: 16 pages, comments are welcome
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

The purpose of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive structural analysis of quantum finite-level systems in the Heisenberg picture, where the evolution of system observables is modeled by bilinear quantum stochastic differential equations (QSDEs). Firstly, real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation and anticommutation relations are characterized, and relative admissibility between different orthonormal Hermitian bases is formulated. Secondly, strongly aligned subspaces are introduced, based on which decoherence-free subsystems (DFSs) are constructed in general orthonormal Hermitian basis as well as the generalized Gell-Mann basis. Thirdly, conditions for the existence of quantum nondemolition (QND) variables are given in terms of both linear systems theory and spectral separation by output-signal observables. Finally, a sufficient condition for quantum back-action-evading (BAE) measurements is established. A four-qubit nearest-neighbor Heisenberg chain with collective dephasing illustrates these structural properties of quantum finite-level systems.

[731] arXiv:2610.30645 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
Ruixuan Deng, Zhengfeng Ji, Jiayu Zhang, Li Zhou
Comments: 87 pages: 12 pages of main text, 4 pages of references, and 71 pages of appendices. Artifact: this https URL
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.

[732] arXiv:2610.30683 (cross-list from stat.ME) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
Jingsong Bai, Ayush Pandey
Subjects: Methodology (stat.ME); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)

Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

[733] arXiv:2610.30752 (cross-list from econ.GN) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Delegation Divide: An Open Index of AI-Agent Delegability across Occupations and Countries
Cristian Espinal Maya (Universidad Nacional de Colombia), Santiago Jiménez Londoño (Universidad EAFIT)
Comments: 32 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Preregistered at OSF: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9ZNTF. Data and code: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23552918%3B repository and MCP server: this https URL
Subjects: General Economics (econ.GN); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

35.2% of task time in world employment is at least partly delegable to AI agents in 2026, and only 2.5% can be handed over in full. Existing measures score exposure to generative AI, mostly for the United States. We build the Agent Delegability Index (ADI): two language models rate all 18,796 O*NET 30.2 task statements on a frozen, preregistered rubric of delegation levels and barriers; tasks are mapped to 433 ISCO-08 unit groups and weighted by ILOSTAT employment in 146 countries. Four findings. First, delegable employment rises with income, from 22.5% in low-income to 48.7% in high-income countries, a slope of 7.23 percentage points per log point of GDP per capita. This delegation divide is compositional: the physical barrier dominates the jobs poorer countries employ most. Second, at the occupation level ADI tracks exposure closely (r = 0.93 with Eloundou et al. and 0.89 with Felten et al.), above the preregistered bound of 0.80; ADI adds delegation levels and barriers on top of exposure, for the world, not a new ranking of occupations. Third, full delegation is rare and peaks for tasks that take a human about twelve minutes (11.8 minutes). Fourth, the preregistered adoption gap is not supported: across 101 countries, delegability and observed AI usage correlate at r = 0.86, and the gap between them is not wider in middle-income countries (p = 0.27). Model agreement is kappa = 0.77; a blind human rating of 300 tasks agrees with the model consensus at kappa = 0.85, and an agentic panel with web search at kappa = 0.87. We release the index, the atlas, the prompts and an MCP server at this https URL.

[734] arXiv:2610.30815 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: xVGAE: A Hierarchical Variational Graph Autoencoder for Exchangeable Graphs
Daniele Micheletti, Federica Zoe Ricci, Erik B. Sudderth
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Graphs play a crucial role in many applications, ranging from drug discovery to social network modeling and astronomy. Generative models for graphs have substantially advanced in recent years, but we identify relatively simple scenarios where state-of-the-art models struggle to converge within a standard compute budget, or exhibit prohibitively slow generation times. We propose a generative architecture that achieves quality competitive with state-of-the-art models and is orders of magnitude faster at generation. Our approach is inspired by the Aldous-Hoover theorem, a classic representation theorem that characterizes any probability distribution of graphs that is invariant to permutations of node indices or exchangeable. This theorem establishes that three ingredients suffice: a graph-level latent variable, a set of exchangeable node-specific latent variables, and a so-called graphon function that maps graph- and node-level variables to the probability of an edge between any node pair. Given a training set of graphs, our exchangeable Variational Graph AutoEncoder (xVGAE) learns an approximation to their underlying graphons, as well as graph- and node-level latent variables. We show that our xVGAE encodes latent representations that correlate with graph- and node-level properties, and can (quickly, in one shot) generate new graphs that closely match key training set statistics.

[735] arXiv:2610.30852 (cross-list from physics.comp-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Stiff source terms inside ADER-DG method
I.S. Popov, A.P. Popova
Comments: 93 pages, 32 figures, 15 tables
Subjects: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph); Mathematical Physics (math-ph); Numerical Analysis (math.NA); Applied Physics (physics.app-ph); Fluid Dynamics (physics.flu-dyn)

ADER-DG numerical method with the LST-DG predictor, when used to solve hyperbolic equations with stiff source terms, exhibits properties characteristic of IMEX computational schemes. With increasing stiffness, characterized by the parameter $z = \nu{\Delta t}^{n} < 0$, the maximum of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}$ of the ADER-DG numerical method increases. In the region of strong stiffness $|z| \gg 1$, a linear increase in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z) \sim |z|$ occurs. In the region of small source terms $|z| \ll 1$, the results $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ transform into known results for the problem $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(0)$ without source terms. In the transition region $|z| \sim 1$, a range of insignificant decrease in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ is discovered. In the linear case, instability is violated precisely when one of the matrix eigenvalues reaches $\lambda = -1$, regardless of the phase $\theta$ of the numerical solution. A rigorous stability theory of the ADER-DG numerical method for stiff problems for arbitrary degree $N$ of basis polynomials is constructed. The stability condition is simplified to solving a polynomial equation for the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}$. Highly accurate dependencies of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(N, z)$ of the ADER-DG method on the parameter $z$ are obtained. A rigorous direct proof of the approximation of the ADER-DG method is presented. Approximation orders $p = N+1$ for arbitrary degrees $N$ are rigorously derived. A set of numerical experiments is carried out to apply the ADER-DG method to solving both a linear advection-reaction equation and the system of Euler equations for a two-component reacting medium. The results obtained in these calculations confirm the theoretical results well.

[736] arXiv:2610.30890 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
Ying Li, Sanyou Wu, Zi Yang, Qiaochu Xu, Yuhao Liu, Zhidi Lin, Michael Minyi Zhang, Petar Djuric, Alexandre H. Thiery
Comments: 22 pages, 3 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.

[737] arXiv:2610.30904 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Assortment optimization under the perception-adjusted Luce model
Gerardo Berbeglia, Mashbat Suzuki, Matthew Tam
Comments: 17 pages, 1 figure
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

The Perception-Adjusted Luce Model (PALM) introduced by by Echenique et al. (2018) is a sequential choice model that can accommodate violations of regularity and choice overload, behaviors not captured by the utility-maximization framework. Flores et al. (2019) studied the assortment problem under the PALM and proved that, for the case of two levels, there is always an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level. They also conjectured that revenue-ordered by levels remain optimal for the general PALM with any number of levels. We resolve this question in the affirmative by showing that every PALM instance admits an optimal assortment that includes, within each level, all products at or above a level-specific revenue threshold. The proof involves first showing how the conjecture which deals with a discrete optimization problem, can be reduced to proving certain property of a related continuous optimization problem. Specifically, we study a continuous refinement of the assortment decision under the same PALM choice rule. Although the refinement permits partial utility selections, we prove it always has an optimum that selects complete revenue tiers. This allows us to show that the assortment problem is polynomial-time solvable when the number of levels is fixed.

[738] arXiv:2610.30910 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: H-2DGS: Height-Field Gaussian Splatting for Sharp and Deformable Neurosurgical Surface Reconstruction
Zhang Zichuan, Bart Brouwers, Rembrandt Bakker, Maud Landers, Geert-Jan Rutten, Maxime Chamberland
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR)

Neurosurgical navigation commonly presents magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as 2D slices, making it difficult to relate the anatomy in those slices to the cortical surface observed through the surgical microscope. We seek a common 3D visualization that combines a photorealistic reconstruction of the exposed cortex during tumor surgery with whole-brain MRI context and diffusion tractography pathways. This requires the reconstructed cortex to form a clear boundary around the brain anatomy rather than a diffuse volume that obscures internal structures. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reproduce observed views but, under limited surgical view coverage, may distribute opacity through a thick and geometrically ambiguous band. We introduce height-field 2D Gaussian Splatting (H-2DGS), a three-stage pipeline that concentrates a robust 3DGS reconstruction, fuses its depth into a shared truncated signed distance field (TSDF) surface, and represents that surface with curved, surface-oriented Gaussian primitives. Separate height, color, and opacity bases provide local geometry and appearance, while a neighbor-transition objective coordinates overlapping patches. The explicit surface further supports postoperative alignment: MRI-derived depth deforms the reconstruction, and tracked-color supervision with alternating optimization preserves its appearance. Across five real neurosurgical cases, H-2DGS gives low multi-view depth inconsistency, a compact 7.97MB representation, and interactive rendering at 29--42ms per frame. The resulting sharp, deformable surface integrates clearly with tractography and MRI anatomy, including a postoperative resection cavity.

[739] arXiv:2610.30940 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, other]
Title: Vision Transformers for Estimating Irradiance Using Data Scarce Sky Images
David Hamlyn, Sunny Chaudhary, Tasmiat Rahman
Journal-ref: Energy and AI 21 (2025), 100560
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Accurate estimation of diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) is critical for optimising photovoltaic system performance and energy forecasting yet remains challenging in regions lacking comprehensive ground-based instrumentation. Recent advancements using Vision Transformers (ViTs) trained on extensive sky image datasets have shown promise in replacing costly irradiance measurement equipment, but the scarcity of long-term, high-quality sky imagery significantly restricts practical implementation. Addressing this critical gap, this study proposes a novel dual-framework approach designed for data-scarce scenarios. First, calculated atmospheric parameters, including extraterrestrial irradiance and cyclic time encodings, are integrated to represent sky conditions without utilising any instrumentation. Next, a sequential pipeline initially predicts synthetic global horizontal irradiance (GHI) and uses it as a feature, to refine DHI estimation. Finally, a dual-parallel architecture simultaneously processes raw and overlay-enhanced fisheye sky images. Overlays are generated through unsupervised, physics-informed cloud segmentation to highlight dynamic sky features. Empirical validation is performed using data from the Chilbolton Observatory, chosen for its temperate climate and frequent cloud variability. To simulate data-scarce conditions, models are trained on a single month (e.g., January) and evaluated across a temporally disjoint, full-year test set. Under this setup, the sequential and dual-parallel frameworks achieve RMSE values within 2-3 W/m^2 and 1-6 W/m^2, respectively, of a state-of-the-art ViT trained on the complete dataset. By combining physics-informed modelling with unsupervised segmentation, the proposed method provides a scalable and cost-effective solution for DHI estimation, advancing solar resource assessment in data-constrained environments.

[740] arXiv:2610.30942 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, other]
Title: GateFormer: Forecast-Space Decomposition for Intra-Hour Solar Irradiance Prediction from Sky Images
David Hamlyn, Sunny Chaudhary, Jonathon Hare, Tasmiat Rahman
Journal-ref: Energy and AI 26 (2026), 100917
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Sub-hourly dispatch, balancing, and storage control increasingly depend on forecasts that anticipate rapid variability in solar generation. Accurate sky-image-based irradiance forecasting requires a combination of visual cloud dynamics with recent irradiance state while adapting to different short-term irradiance-change regimes. To address this, we introduce GateFormer, a GHI-conditioned dual-decoder ViT for intra-hour global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting through forecast-space decomposition. GateFormer embeds observed GHI into the visual token stream, allowing interaction with sky-image patch features through self-attention. From this shared representation, a Trajectory Head predicts future GHI sequence, while a Delta Head predicts final-horizon change from the latest observed GHI. The two final-horizon forecasts are adaptively weighted in prediction space, with magnitude- and direction-supervision targeting the remaining error. On the NREL-TSI benchmark, GateFormer attains 125.01 W/m^2 RMSE at +30 min, improving over a state-of-the-art transformer baseline by 9.6% under paired-timestamp evaluation. Across NREL-TSI, Chilbolton, and SIRTA, GateFormer achieves the lowest final-horizon RMSE among the evaluated baselines, with forecast skill of 22.97-28.86% relative to smart persistence. Component ablations show adaptive weighting outperforms both individual decoders and fixed averaging, distinguishing GateFormer from conventional forecast combination, while the supervised correction further reduces RMSE by 1.68 W/m^2 and MAE by 4.86 W/m^2. Ramp-regime diagnostics show larger gains during operationally important positive ramps, reducing RMSE by 26.27 W/m^2. These results identify forecast-space decomposition as an alternative forecasting formulation, with potential relevance to other multimodal short-horizon forecasting tasks and deployment using only sky images and measured GHI.

[741] arXiv:2610.30948 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Random Projections for Spectral Algorithms: Optimal Rates in Sobolev Norms
Caixing Wang, Yue Wang
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Random projections (RP) offer an effective method for reducing computational and storage overhead while preserving the geometric structure of data. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the optimal generalization performance of specific kernel-regularized algorithms with RP in the well-specified setting and under restrictive conditions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of the generalization performance of RP-based spectral algorithms under general conditions \change{without sacrificing statistical efficiency}. By leveraging the embedding property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and a refined analysis of the operator similarity, we establish optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms that match the minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. For two common implementations of RP, randomized sketches and Nyström sub-sampling (uniform or leverage-based), we show that the projection dimension required for optimality is proportional to the average or maximal effective dimension, yielding a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining the statistical efficiency. Our results do not rely on the uniform boundedness assumption on the regression function and are valid across a wide range of source conditions, i.e., $s> \alpha_0-1/\beta$, where $s,\beta$, and $\alpha_0$ denote the smoothness index, capacity index, and the embedding index, respectively. In the benign case when $\alpha_0=1/\beta$, the optimality holds for all $s\in (0,2\tau]$ with $\tau$ and $\gamma$ denoting the qualification index and norm index. Experimental results demonstrate both the theoretical validity and the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.

[742] arXiv:2610.30966 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Bound-Conditioned Latent Inference for Progressive Image Compression
Jaeseok Jang, Seungmin Jeon, Kwang Pyo Choi, Chang-Su Kim
Comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Progressive image compression reconstructs images from prefixes of a single bitstream and therefore involves sequential latent inference under partial observations. Existing trit-plane codecs mainly treat decoded trits as discrete symbols for probability prediction, without fully exploiting their role as interval constraints on the underlying continuous latents. We propose bound-conditioned latent inference (BLI), a framework that reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints. At each coding step, the trits decoded so far define lower and upper bounds for each latent element. BLI uses the center and width of these bounds, together with hyperprior information shared by the encoder and decoder, to jointly refine the Gaussian parameters $(\mu,\sigma)$ for entropy modeling and the latent estimate $\hat{y}$ for reconstruction. As additional trits are decoded, the feasible intervals shrink monotonically, yielding tighter constraints for the next inference step and enabling flexible in-plane refinement schedules. Experiments on Kodak, CLIC, and JPEG-AI show that BLI achieves state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among progressive image codecs, reducing BD-rate by $17.78\%$ over DPICT and by $7.96\%$ over CTC on Kodak, while replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about $5.3\times$ fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC.

[743] arXiv:2610.30967 (cross-list from math.GN) [pdf, html, other]
Title: On U_c-admitting spaces and U_c-completions of T_0 spaces
Kangming Lu, Qingguo Li, Shengwen Wang, Rongqi Xiao
Subjects: General Topology (math.GN); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

In this paper, we introduce a new class of spaces, termed U_c-admitting spaces, and investigate their relationships with U_s-admitting spaces and well-filtered spaces. Adopting the perspective of H-sobriety, we show that every U_c-admitting space is H-sober, so that U_c-admitting spaces arise as a special case of H-sober spaces. Consequently, the category U_c-Sob of U_c-admitting spaces and continuous maps is complete and forms a reflective subcategory of Top_0. In addition, we prove that a T_0 space X is U_c-admitting if and only if its Smyth power space is U_c-admitting. Finally, we present the standard U_c-completion of an arbitrary T_0 space.

[744] arXiv:2610.31042 (cross-list from stat.CO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Sequential Monte Carlo Sampling of Feasible Regions Represented by R-Functions
Sinan Yıldırım, Sergei Kucherenko
Comments: 22 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables
Subjects: Computation (stat.CO); Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

Feasible-region sampling and volume estimation become increasingly inefficient when constraints define only a small fraction of a convenient bounding domain. We combine R-functions, which encode compound feasibility as a continuous signed field, with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers. The proposed construction exploits not only the sign of the R-function, which determines exact feasibility, but also its continuous negative values outside the feasible set, which provide graded information on constraint violation. Logistic intermediate distributions use this information to guide particles progressively towards feasibility, while the final target distribution remains uniform on the feasible region.
Experiments on intersections and unions, including disconnected cases of hyperballs, show substantial variance reductions relative to direct rejection sampling, with the statistical advantage generally increasing as the feasible fraction decreases. For sufficiently small feasible regions, these advantages persist even after accounting for computational cost. To isolate the benefit of continuous R-function information, we also compare the proposed method with an SMC sampler with a region-only (RO) construction that uses the same sequential particle machinery but retains only binary feasible/infeasible information. We demonstrate that the R-function-informed SMC method concentrates particles in the feasible region earlier and produces lower-variance volume estimates than RO.

[745] arXiv:2610.31136 (cross-list from eess.SP) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Array Rotation in Near-Field ISAC: Communication, Detection, and Estimation Under Low-Complexity Transmit Architectures
Marziyeh Soltani, Mark F. Flanagan
Subjects: Signal Processing (eess.SP); Information Theory (cs.IT)

This paper studies near-field integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) with a rotatable base-station array under an exact spherical-wave propagation model. For a general transmit covariance, we derive a Cramér--Rao bound (CRB) decomposition that separates target-side geometry from transmit-covariance-dependent terms. We then specialize the framework to two representative low-complexity architectures: a single-stream superposition architecture, and a dual-waveform split architecture design. We characterize the communication-, detection-, and estimation-optimal rotations for each architecture using the exact finite-array model. In addition, we show how a second-order approximation yields compact approximate expressions for the optimal rotation angles. We also study uncertainty in the target state used for beamforming design through a correlated Gaussian perturbation model, and derive approximations of the optimal robust rotation angles for target sensing and detection. The analysis shows that the two architectures behave differently under rotation: the single-stream design can align communication and detection tasks, whereas the dual-waveform design exhibits a direct communication--detection tradeoff and can incur a larger communication loss when sensing is prioritized. Numerical results show clear gains over a fixed array orientation, especially for range estimation, and close agreement between the approximate and exact rotation choices. Detection is less affected by target-state errors than estimation in the considered cases.

[746] arXiv:2610.31163 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, other]
Title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
Ryan Heejoon Byun, Dayeon Yoon, Won Chang
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Applications (stat.AP); Computation (stat.CO); Methodology (stat.ME)

Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

[747] arXiv:2610.31164 (cross-list from math.PR) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A local-to-global principle for $f$-divergence homogenization
Aryeh Kontorovich
Subjects: Probability (math.PR); Information Theory (cs.IT)

We study the effect of replacing a family of independent statistical experiments by independent repetitions of their average. We give a simple, complete characterization of the $f$-divergences for which this operation increases divergence by at most a constant depending only on the generator, uniformly in the number of observations and the underlying measurable space. The characterization is governed by a local-to-global principle: a comparison restricted to two observations on a binary alphabet already determines the validity of the general inequality. It admits an explicit scalar formulation, which simplifies further for symmetric divergences. The result applies to arbitrary convex generators and requires no differentiability or symmetry assumptions. It recovers the homogenization inequality for total variation and identifies exactly the admissible members of the power-divergence family. In particular, whenever uniform homogenization fails, the obstruction is already present in a family of binary experiments with two observations. Moreover, the global comparison constant is controlled uniformly over generators with a common bound in the local inequality.

[748] arXiv:2610.31165 (cross-list from physics.soc-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
Roberto Passaro, Ariel Flint, Romualdo Pastor-Satorras, Andrea Baronchelli, Luca Maria Aiello
Subjects: Physics and Society (physics.soc-ph); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.

[749] arXiv:2610.31180 (cross-list from physics.data-an) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
Shuhang Li, Haiwang Yu, Gabor Galgoczi, Yeonju Go, Yi Huang, David Park, Michael Peters, Christof Roland, Jin Huang, Yihui Ren, Joseph D. Osborn
Subjects: Data Analysis, Statistics and Probability (physics.data-an); Machine Learning (cs.LG); High Energy Physics - Experiment (hep-ex); Nuclear Experiment (nucl-ex)

Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.

[750] arXiv:2610.31218 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: QICOM: Open-Source Software for Reproducible Image Quality Evaluation, Blinded Assessment, and Radiomic Comparison
Fabio Mattiussi, Switinder Ghotra
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

QICOM (Quality Image COMparator) is open-source software for quantitative image comparison, paired radiomics, and blinded assessment. It saves processing settings, image identities, measurements, and response mappings so a comparison can be reopened and recalculated. We evaluate reference agreement, responses to controlled perturbations, and recovery of saved analyses. Synthetic experiments cover 37 quantitative descriptors using independentnumerical references and separate upstream integration comparisons. The QICOM/MIRP backend meets the reference tolerances for all 482 numeric IBSI 1 digital-phantom entries and all 1,622 entries across configurations A-E of the public CT reference case; these comprise 1,804 feature/aggregation comparisons and 300 preprocessing diagnostics. Restricting masked SSIM and HFEN to complete kernel support removes the observed dependence on excluded pixels. In a synthetic filtering example, stronger smoothing increases SSIM while worsening MSE and HFEN relative to milder smoothing and changing GLCM contrast more strongly. Reopened radiomics projects reproduce all 43 feature pairs per comparison, and two blinded deliveries return four correctly mapped scripted responses. These experiments document the calculations and data transfers linking the three workflows.

[751] arXiv:2610.31260 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
Ravi Kumar Jha, Hsuan-Yin Lin, Eirik Rosnes
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.

[752] arXiv:2610.31298 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Strong Duality Thresholds and Minimum Curvature for the Nearest Rectangular Symplectic Matrix Problem
Yulin Xie, Aiqing Zhu, Yifa Tang
Comments: 20 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We study the nearest rectangular symplectic matrix problem in the squared Frobenius norm for arbitrary targets $T\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2k}$, with $n\ge k$. We prove that its semidefinite relaxation is exact for every target if and only if $n\ge2k-1$. Under this condition, the primal problem, the relaxation, and both Lagrangian dual problems attain the same optimal value. In this range, we derive the exact minimum Rayleigh quotient of the Riemannian Hessian at every feasible point under the Euclidean induced metric, and prove that all second-order stationary points are global minimizers. We also obtain global objective error bounds. We extend the strong-duality and minimum-curvature results to Hermitian positive definite row weights, proving that strong duality holds for every target if and only if the lowest eigenvalue of the weight has complex multiplicity at least $2k-1$. The dual formulation leads to a method whose main iterations use matrices of order $2k$, with $O(k^2)$ iterative storage apart from the full input and output. Across six tested sizes, mean-time speedups are $2.55$--$12.60$ over a Riemannian first-order method and $4.61$--$43.93$ over Jensen--Zimmermann R--TR2; batching gives a further factor of $3.45$--$23.53$ over sequential calls. The theoretical results complete the critical dimensions not covered by Gram convexification and quadratic matrix programming.

[753] arXiv:2610.31328 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
Marcos Matabuena, Xiaokai Luo, Oscar Hernan Madrid Padilla
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST); Methodology (stat.ME)

Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

[754] arXiv:2610.31335 (cross-list from math.HO) [pdf, other]
Title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
Igor' Kontorovich, Miriam N. Wallach
Comments: 44 pages. Preprint under consideration at Digital Experiences in Mathematics Education; not peer reviewed
Subjects: History and Overview (math.HO); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

[755] arXiv:2610.31336 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
Rui Qiu, Fang Yao, Zhou Yu
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.

[756] arXiv:2610.31350 (cross-list from cond-mat.str-el) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Graph-Recurrent Learning of Emergent Collective Dynamics
Ali Rayat, Acacia Lee, Gia-Wei Chern
Comments: 13 pages, 8 figures
Subjects: Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Collective ordering in correlated electron systems emerges from microscopic dynamics, yet the evolution of observable textures need not admit a closed, memoryless description. We introduce a graph-recurrent neural network (GRNN) framework that learns such emergent dynamics directly from trajectories without specifying microscopic equations of motion. The framework integrates gated recurrent memory with graph message passing: local hidden states encode information beyond the instantaneous observables, while spatial coupling allows this information to propagate between sites. The observable and hidden fields evolve jointly through a shared local rule, providing a scalable representation of dynamics with spatial interactions and temporal memory. We demonstrate this framework on the emergent dynamics of charge-density-wave order in the semiclassical Holstein model, successfully reproducing temporal and spatial correlations and dynamical scaling during domain coarsening. By learning finite-time evolution directly, the GRNN offers a route to efficient, data-driven descriptions of collective dynamics with unresolved microscopic degrees of freedom.

[757] arXiv:2610.31359 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Finite Systems in the Space of Projective Measurements
Miguel Flores R., Carlos A. Muñoz
Comments: 15 pages, 13 figures, 27 images
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET)

We investigate the dynamics of two-level systems using the quasidistribution $Q$ function projected onto the space of collective measurements. Particular attention is given to evolution under Hamiltonians that are invariant under particle permutations, for pure states that are either invariant or noninvariant under such permutations. This requires constructing an approximate analog of the star product between quasidistribution functions: the projected $Q$ function of a product of two operators is expressed approximately in terms of the individual operators' $Q$ and $P$ functions. We rewrite the Liouville equation to determine approximate state dynamics and compare the result with exact evolution using the Hellinger distance. Overall, the method performs well for permutation-invariant pure states and Hamiltonians, whereas deviations arise for arbitrary pure states and noninvariant Hamiltonians.

[758] arXiv:2610.31362 (cross-list from math.CO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A new lower bound for the sixth Schur number: $S(6)\ge 537$
Zhiyang Chen, Ligeng Zhu, Fan Long
Subjects: Combinatorics (math.CO); Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM)

We give an explicit partition of $\{1,\ldots,537\}$ into six sum-free sets, establishing $S(6)\ge 537$. This improves the lower bound 536 of Fredricksen and Sweet (2000). Known recursive constructions then give the improved lower bounds $S(8)\ge 5\,372$, $S(11)\ge 204\,208$, $S(13)\ge 2\,042\,082$, and $R_6(3)\ge 539$. We also report 131 pairwise inequivalent partitions found by the search. We describe their structure and provide the complete partitions in the supplementary material. These partitions provide starting points for future searches and structural studies of Schur partitions.

[759] arXiv:2610.31364 (cross-list from physics.flu-dyn) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A second-order linear decoupled scheme with a relaxed zero-energy variable for Rayleigh-Bénard convection
Matthew McCurdy
Comments: 38 pages, 10 figures
Subjects: Fluid Dynamics (physics.flu-dyn); Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We construct a second-order, linear, and fully decoupled scheme for Rayleigh--Bénard convection between Navier-slip walls. The nonlinear terms are treated explicitly and multiplied by a scalar with exact value $1$ and no energy contributed to the continuous problem. As a result, each BDF2 step, with a rotational pressure correction, solves only constant-coefficient linear problems. For the time discretization, we prove that, for any time-step, the energy decays when the walls have equal temperatures, under a condition on the thermal weight, and the energy is bounded on finite time intervals when heated from below. Relaxing the scalar towards $1$ preserves both estimates. Energy stability does not control the accuracy of the scalar; the velocity and temperature fields are computed with its unrelaxed value, whose deviation from $1$ scales like $(E/C)(\delta t/\tau)^3$ for kinetic energy $E$, time-scale $\tau$ of the flow, and weight $C$ of the scalar equation. In our tests, choosing $C$ comparable to $E$ keeps this deviation small and doubles the largest time-step for which steady rolls are reproduced to a relative difference of $10^{-8}$. With Taylor--Hood elements, we observe second-order convergence in time, recover the critical Rayleigh numbers, and match published Nusselt numbers to within $0.5\%$. A three-dimensional implementation passes corresponding validation tests.

[760] arXiv:2610.31391 (cross-list from math.AT) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Bridging persistence of discrete and continuous 1D maps: Total variation, permutation equivalence, and diagonal affine transformations
Matthew Blake, Firas A. Khasawneh
Comments: 60 pages, 24 figures
Subjects: Algebraic Topology (math.AT); Computational Geometry (cs.CG)

Fundamental to the field of topological signal processing (TSP) is the \textit{persistence diagram} (PD), or barcode, of a signal, which gives noise-resistant measures of topologically significant features as distinct from noise. Existing literature proves that the total persistence computed from these diagrams is equal to the total variation, for certain continuous signals on compact domains. We provide a closed formula for this shared quantity, and generalize to all continuous and discrete functions on bounded domains, and to certain functions on non-compact 1D manifolds. Extending the identification of continuous and discrete persistence, we investigate the similarities of functions with the same PDs, and prove that, for any $n$, the persistence diagram can be calculated as a function of the sequence of critical values; we compute these formulas for $n \leq 6$. Finally, we examine which function transformations cause predictable changes in the PD of the transformed function, characterizing affine and linear transformations.

[761] arXiv:2610.31418 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Resource Allocation Tournament
Adam Nathaniel, Refael Hassin
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Theoretical Economics (econ.TH)
