We introduce and analyze a round-robin simultaneous resource allocation contest, motivated by sports leagues and other competitive environments where agents must distribute limited resources across multiple encounters. Players allocate resources in advance to matches against all opponents, and match outcomes are determined by relative allocations. We study two payoff schemes: total points, where players accumulate rewards for each win, and winner-takes-all, where only the tournament winner is rewarded. For three players, we provide complete equilibrium characterizations under both schemes. For four or more players, we show that the total points payoff admits Blotto-type equilibria, while the winner-takes-all payoff requires numerical and algorithmic analysis. To address this, we develop a best-response dynamics algorithm with stochastic inertia and use it to approximate equilibria in games with four and five players.

[762] arXiv:2610.31431 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
Yuansi Chen, Francesco Pedrotti, Peter A. Whalley
Comments: 30 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Probability (math.PR); Statistics Theory (math.ST); Computation (stat.CO)

The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.

[763] arXiv:2610.31443 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: ConQEC: Concolic Testing for Quantum Error-Correcting Code Implementations
Zihao Li, Ji Guan, Mingsheng Ying
Comments: 12 pages. Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027)
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Quantum error-correcting code (QECC) implementations are hybrid software-control systems: measured syndromes drive decoder dispatch, recovery actions, and logical checks. Existing QECC verification techniques can prove formal obligations, and general quantum testing can expose final failures, but developers still lack a scalable testing workflow that generates concrete faults and explains where a QECC repair path first diverges. This paper presents ConQEC, to our knowledge the first concolic testing framework for QECC implementations. By combining concrete (Pauli) fault replay with symbolic repair-path constraints, ConQEC generates tests that expose not only final logical failures but also fault--syndrome--decoder--recovery (FSDR) diagnostics: the injected fault, observed syndrome, decoder decision, recovery action, oracle result, and earliest divergent stage. Its symbolic encoding of Pauli faults, syndrome predicates, decoder and recovery relations, and oracle checks enables this diagnostic workflow to scale beyond exponentially increasing amplitude-level quantum-state reasoning. We implemented ConQEC and evaluated it on generated source-level QECC families and public QECC artifacts with up to thousands of qubits. ConQEC detects the seeded bug in every experimental case and reports a replay-valid, fault-localizing FSDR witness for each.

[764] arXiv:2610.31490 (cross-list from eess.IV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Self-Supervised Multibeam Sonar Restoration via Coherent Forward Modeling
Zixin Wang, James Hopgood, Mike Davies
Comments: 16 pages, 8 figures, includes supplementary material
Subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Signal Processing (eess.SP)

Multibeam imaging sonar produces intensity images degraded by coherent speckle and system-induced blur, while clean reflectivity targets are rarely available. Existing despeckling methods often rely on simplified intensity-domain noise models, synthetic clean targets, or blind-spot self-supervision, and typically do not jointly model deblurring and speckle suppression.
We propose a physics-consistent self-supervised framework for joint despeckling and deblurring of multibeam imaging sonar. A stochastic coherent image-formation model yields a conditional-mean forward operator that relates latent scene reflectivity to expected intensity through the squared magnitude of the system point spread function. We then use registered multi-frame sonar sequences to train without clean ground truth images, showing that, under an idealized inter-frame conditional-mean condition, the expected paired loss equals the corresponding forward-prediction loss up to a network-independent constant. To stabilize the ill-conditioned inverse problem, we further adapt robust equivariant imaging using stochastic coherent simulation and introduce a paired forward prediction error metric for ground-truth-free evaluation. Experiments on two real multibeam sonar datasets demonstrate a favourable balance between forward-prediction agreement, homogeneous-region speckle suppression, and preservation of visible structural boundaries compared with representative baselines.

[765] arXiv:2610.31501 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: One-shot entanglement generation and distillation via Petz recovery and binary hypothesis testing
Matthew Can, Mark M. Wilde
Comments: 53 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Information Theory (cs.IT)

How much entanglement can two distant laboratories share when their connection is noisy? We relate this question to deciding which of two quantum hypotheses is present. Our one-shot bounds apply to entanglement generation over a quantum channel and to one-way entanglement distillation from a shared state. We use Cheng's trace inequality to bound the infidelity of a Petz decoder in terms of a binary hypothesis testing cost. Applying the inequality before averaging over codes reduces the error analysis to computing a second moment of random subspaces. The proof covers every integer target dimension and treats rank-deficient states explicitly. A corollary expresses the achievable entanglement through hypothesis-testing coherent information, with a single logarithmic error slack and exact integer rounding. We also prove an error-preserving conversion from entanglement generation codes to entanglement transmission codes: the target dimension decreases by only a constant factor at fixed error, and the decoder is the original decoder followed by local processing. Consequently, for both entanglement generation and entanglement transmission, arbitrary pure reference-input states yield the same coherent-information rate, second-order Gaussian correction at the original error tolerance, and explicit achievable logarithmic remainder. For commuting testing hypotheses, the logarithmic remainder improves to a constant. These results give a direct route from binary distinguishability to explicit recovery guarantees and finite-resource quantum communication rates.

[766] arXiv:2610.31524 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Nonparametric autoregressive estimation of probability distributions with parallel gradient boosting
Rémy Chapelle (CB, EVDG, CESP)
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Nonparametric estimation of joint probability distributions is a core problem in statistics, which is notoriously challenging with high-dimensional data. Such challenges also arise with conditional distribution estimation and have led to flexible algorithms that aim to tackle the ''curse of dimensionality'' by exploiting predictive structures of lower dimension than the ambient space. In this paper, we study the use of such conditional distribution estimators to estimate joint distributions by factorizing the latter in an ''autoregressive'' way. We show that for loss functions satisfying a subadditivity property, bounds on the convergence rate of an autoregressive estimator can be derived from bounds on the convergence rate of the conditional distribution estimators. These bounds relate the difficulty of estimating the joint distribution to that of estimating the most challenging factor in the autoregressive factorization. When the conditional estimators adapt to sparsity in their conditioning sets, we characterize this difficulty through variable elimination in an undirected dependence graph. This allows bounding the rates of convergence by quantities related to the sparsity of the graph, and provides an additional motivation for the autoregressive approach. We then evaluate the practical performance of an autoregressive estimator based on parallel gradient boosting, a flexible nonparametric method for estimating conditional distributions. The estimator demonstrates competitive estimation performance on various simulated and real datasets, even without optimizing the factorization order. Together, these results support nonparametric autoregressive estimation as a practical approach to flexible joint distribution estimation.

[767] arXiv:2610.31526 (cross-list from math.OC) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
Lorenzo Sabug Jr., Eric Kerrigan
Comments: 27 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.

[768] arXiv:2610.31554 (cross-list from quant-ph) [pdf, html, other]
Title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation
Zhengyi Liu, Li Liu, Songtao Liu, Xianglong Liu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Mingyu Huang, Dingchao Gao, Shenggang Ying, Ji Guan, Bolong Chen
Comments: 29 pages, 4 figures, 15 tables. Code and benchmarks: this https URL
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Mathematical Software (cs.MS)

Tensor-network simulation of quantum circuits depends on contraction orders with low computational cost and small intermediate tensors, found without excessive planning time. We present ArcTN, a contraction-order optimization framework with two search presets. Light keeps planning overhead low, and Heavy spends more effort on refinement. Both combine randomized-greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering with stage-specific stopping rules. ArcTN also provides Fixed and Dynamic slicing to meet tensor-size limits and executes the returned orders. On the 30 QC32 quantum-circuit networks completed by all eight compared configurations, Light reduces FLOPs by 61.32% and plans 1.62$\times$ faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA-ES, and Heavy reduces FLOPs by 43.83% and plans 7.21$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ/Optuna. Heavy also needs 11.85% fewer FLOPs than OMECO TreeSA-8 and plans 1.33$\times$ faster. Dynamic slicing meets the size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar-output networks and reduces total sliced FLOPs by 31.99% relative to Fixed slicing, at the cost of longer planning. With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. On 672 networks built from 320 MQT Bench circuits, Heavy obtains the lowest geometric-mean FLOPs on the 142 large networks while planning 3.1$\times$ and 31$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ and Hyper128.

[769] arXiv:2610.31662 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
Isaac Gibbs, Elise L. Han, Ryan J. Tibshirani, Tijana Zrnic
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Methodology (stat.ME)

We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

Replacement submissions (showing 418 of 418 entries)

[770] arXiv:1409.6247 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Distributional Learning of Context-Free Languages under Fixed Finite-Semigroup Typing
Takayuki Kuriyama
Comments: 26 pages. v5: substantially revised version. Typing is now by a finite-semigroup morphism on nonempty factors (title changed accordingly); the learning algorithm is corrected by separating a set-driven reconstruction operator from a conservative Gold learner; new exponential lower bound on characteristic data for a two-element semilattice typing; manuscript reorganized and shortened
Subjects: Formal Languages and Automata Theory (cs.FL)

We study positive-data learning of context-free languages whose nonempty factors are typed by a fixed morphism $s:\Sigma^+\to S$ into a finite semigroup. A polynomial-time set-driven operator reconstructs each substitutable target from finite positive witnesses; a separate conservative learner identifies nonempty targets in Gold's sense. The encoded characteristic-data size is polynomial in grammar size and a typed shortest-yield parameter. Ordinary grammar thickness suffices when the typing is determined by a fixed prefix-suffix window and a finite-group value; for linear targets, linear grammar size alone suffices. Conversely, a fixed two-element semilattice typing yields finite targets with grammars of size and ordinary thickness both $O(n)$ that require exponentially long characteristic samples. The lower bound applies to any set-driven operator admitting characteristic samples for the fixed-typing class. Retyping closure, examples beyond fixed windows, and a Dyck-language obstruction delineate the framework's scope.

[771] arXiv:1502.05056 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: On Sex, Evolution, and the Multiplicative Weights Update Algorithm
Reshef Meir, David Parkes
Comments: full version of a paper accepted to AAMAS-2015
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

We consider a recent innovative theory by Chastain et al. on the role of sex in evolution [PNAS'14]. In short, the theory suggests that the evolutionary process of gene recombination implements the celebrated multiplicative weights updates algorithm (MWUA). They prove that the population dynamics induced by sexual reproduction can be precisely modeled by genes that use MWUA as their learning strategy in a particular coordination game. The result holds in the environments of \emph{weak selection}, under the assumption that the population frequencies remain a product distribution.
We revisit the theory, eliminating both the requirement of weak selection and any assumption on the distribution of the population. Removing the assumption of product distributions is crucial, since as we show, this assumption is inconsistent with the population dynamics. We show that the marginal allele distributions induced by the population dynamics precisely match the marginals induced by a multiplicative weights update algorithm in this general setting, thereby affirming and substantially generalizing these earlier results.
We further revise the implications for convergence and utility or fitness guarantees in coordination games. In contrast to the claim of Chastain et al.[PNAS'14], we conclude that the sexual evolutionary dynamics does not entail any property of the population distribution, beyond those already implied by convergence.

[772] arXiv:1803.03407 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Anchoring Distributed Agency: Institutional Metaphors for Designing Large-Scale AI and AI Techniques for Running Institutions
Alexander Boer, Giovanni Sileno
Comments: invited chapter. major update since the first version in 2018, before camera-ready version
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Artificial Intelligence (AI) started out with the ambition to reproduce the human mind, but as soon as the sheer scale of that ambition became apparent, it retreated into either studying specialized intelligent behaviours or proposing overarching architectural concepts for interfacing specialized intelligent components---conceived of as agents acting through organizational structures. The agent-based modelling paradigm proved to have interesting applications beyond the original domain, supporting the understanding, simulation, and the assessment of behaviour of socio-economic and legal structures on an aggregate level. Looking at contemporary AI, whereas text completion provides a successful example of specialized behaviour, surprisingly little of the rich foundation of multi-agent systems (MAS) and normative systems research is currently reflected in Agentic AI systems. Addressing this gap, the chapter examines cross-cutting conceptualisations, modelling problems, and design challenges shared by large-scale distributed AI and institutional systems. Three main contributions can be highlighted. First, by tracing the historical trajectory of AI, the chapter identifies an \textit{ecological} perspective on intelligence, examining both the value and limits of the \textit{compression-as-intelligence} hypothesis. Second, it shows how moving between internal cognitive mechanisms and external manifestations of agency supports a functional separation of concerns for both individual and collective agency. Third, it argues that \textit{epistemological}, \textit{normative}, and \textit{value pluralisms} are necessary conditions for sustaining the ecological character of intelligence. Furthermore, we indicate how AI techniques can support institutions by modelling social roles, simulating normative interactions, detecting and diagnosing failures, and supporting procedures of review and revision.

[773] arXiv:2003.00545 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Selling to Non-linear Agents: A Demand-Based Auction
Yiding Feng, Jason Hartline, Yingkai Li
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Theoretical Economics (econ.TH)

Auctions allocate scarce goods, from car licenses to online advertising, to buyers whose utilities are often not linear in money, as with budgets or risk aversion. We ask how a seller should sell to such buyers and what learning their preferences is worth. We propose demand-based auctions, which elicit demand curves and are dominant-strategy incentive compatible for any non-linear utilities. The revenue-maximizing one takes familiar second-price forms and is max-min optimal when the seller observes only demand curves. Under standard assumptions, learning risk attitudes beyond demand curves adds relatively little revenue, as does learning budgets unless they correlate with values.

[774] arXiv:2207.12084 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: ASA: A Simulation Environment for Evaluating Military Operational Scenarios
Joao P. A. Dantas, Andre N. Costa, Vitor C. F. Gomes, Andre R. Kuroswiski, Felipe L. L. Medeiros, Diego Geraldo, Adrisson R. Samersla, Samara R. Silva, Andre F. M. Caetano, Yuri D. Ferreira, Alessandro O. Arantes, Davison S. Santos, Marcia R. C. Aquino
Comments: 13 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Published in Computational Science and Computational Intelligence (CSCI 2024), Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2512, Springer, 2025
Journal-ref: Computational Science and Computational Intelligence (CSCI 2024), Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2512, pp. 203-215, Springer, Cham (2025)
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

The Aerospace Simulation Environment (Ambiente de Simulação Aeroespacial -- ASA in Portuguese) is a custom-made object-oriented simulation framework developed mainly in C++ that enables the modeling and simulation of military operational scenarios to support the development of tactics and procedures in the aerospace context for the Brazilian Air Force. This work describes the ASA framework and its main features: a distributed architecture for coordinating multiple simulation machines, a modular structure that allows models to be loaded at runtime, a batch execution mode for simulating multiple scenarios with varied initial conditions, and an integrated data analysis platform for post-processing simulation results. In addition, we present a list of recent studies that have used ASA in applications related to decision support and autonomy in air combat scenarios.

[775] arXiv:2303.03538 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Evolutionary Deep Nets for Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring
Jinsong Wang, Kenneth A. Loparo
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Signal Processing (eess.SP); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Compact appliance classifiers can support local electricity-load monitoring where memory and computation are constrained. We evaluate adaptive sparse evolutionary training and warm-start compression using synthetic aggregate windows derived from household appliance recordings. A completed convolutional network study trains 120 models over four targets and three seeds with validation-only model selection. Two analyses examine compression with approximately preserved binary accuracy and joint improvement in positive-class F1 and sparsity. Relative to a newly trained fixed sparse evolutionary baseline, the selected compressed policy changes accuracy from 91.53%, while increasing macro F1 to 92.40%. Stored weights decrease by 17.36% and active first-layer connections by 23.93%. Refinement requires additional training. Three seeds and unverified source-window independence prevent claims of statistical equivalence or unseen-house performance.

[776] arXiv:2401.15857 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Opinion Dynamics in Social Multiplex Networks with Mono and Bi-directional Interactions in the Presence of Leaders
Amirreza Talebi, Sayed Pedram Haeri Boroujeni, Abolfazl Razi
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

We delve into the dynamics of opinions within a multiplex network using coordination games, where agents communicate either through one-way or two-way interactions, and where a designated leader may be present. By employing graph theory and Markov chains, we illustrate that despite zero diagonal elements in transition probability matrices or decomposable layers, opinions converge under specific conditions on the layers, leading to a consensus, and we show by a counterexample that a spanning tree in the union of the layers does not suffice. We further scrutinize the convergence rates of opinion dynamics in networks with one-way versus two-way interactions. We find that in networks with a designated leader, opinions converge towards the initial opinion of the leader, whereas in networks without a designated leader, opinions converge to a convex combination of the opinions of agents. Moreover, we emphasize the crucial role of designated leaders in steering opinion convergence within the network. Paired experiments on 1,200 random multiplex networks show that a leader slows down convergence, and that two-way interactions slow it down in the presence of a leader but speed it up in its absence.

[777] arXiv:2403.17147 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
Leo Cazenille, Nicolas Lobato-Dauzier, Alessia Loi, Loona Macabre, Mika Ito, Olivier Marchal, Soo-Hyeon Kim, Nathanael Aubert-Kato, Nicolas Bredeche, Anthony J. Genot
Journal-ref: Science Robotics 11 (119), eadr9578 (2026)
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computational Geometry (cs.CG)

Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm's geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse-connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.

[778] arXiv:2404.06966 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Are EEG Sequences Time Series? EEG Classification with Time Series Models and Joint Subject Training
Johannes Burchert, Thorben Werner, Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi, Diego Coello de Portugal, Maximilian Stubbemann, Lars Schmidt-Thieme
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Signal Processing (eess.SP)

As with most other data domains, EEG data analysis relies on rich domain-specific preprocessing. Beyond such preprocessing, machine learners would hope to deal with such data as with any other time series data. For EEG classification many models have been developed with layer types and architectures we typically do not see in time series classification. Furthermore, typically separate models for each individual subject are learned, not one model for all of them. In this paper, we systematically study the differences between EEG classification models and generic time series classification models. We describe three different model setups to deal with EEG data from different subjects, subject-specific models (most EEG literature), subject-agnostic models and subject-conditional models. In experiments on three datasets, we demonstrate that off-the-shelf time series classification models trained per subject perform close to EEG classification models, but that do not quite reach the performance of domain-specific modeling. Additionally, we combine time-series models with subject embeddings to train one joint subject-conditional classifier on all subjects. The resulting models are competitive with dedicated EEG models in 2 out of 3 datasets, even outperforming all EEG methods on one of them.

[779] arXiv:2405.00273 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Social Life Simulation for Non-Cognitive Skills Learning
Zihan Yan, Yaohong Xiang, Yun Huang
Comments: Violation of the institution's Institutional Review Board protocol
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

Non-cognitive skills are crucial for personal and social life well-being, and such skill development can be supported by narrative-based (e.g., storytelling) technologies. While generative AI enables interactive and role-playing storytelling, little is known about how users engage with and perceive the use of AI in social life simulation for non-cognitive skills learning. Additionally, the benefits of AI mentorship on self-reflection awareness and ability in this context remain largely underexplored. To this end, we introduced Simulife++, an interactive platform enabled by a large language model (LLM). The system allows users to act as protagonists, creating stories with one or multiple AI-based characters in diverse social scenarios. In particular, we expanded the Human-AI interaction to a Human-AI-AI collaboration by including a Sage Agent, who acts as a bystander, providing users with some perspectives and guidance on their choices and conversations in terms of non-cognitive skills to promote reflection. In a within-subject user study, our quantitative results reveal that, when accompanied by Sage Agent, users exhibit significantly higher levels of reflection on motivation, self-perceptions, and resilience & coping, along with an enhanced experience of narrative transportation. Additionally, our qualitative findings suggest that Sage Agent plays a crucial role in promoting reflection on non-cognitive skills, enhancing social communication and decision-making performance, and improving overall user experience within Simulife++. Multiple supportive relationships between Sage Agent and users were also reported. We offer design implications for the application of generative AI in narrative solutions and the future potential of Sage Agent for non-cognitive skill development in broader social contexts.

[780] arXiv:2405.13795 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Memory-Efficient Distributed Algorithm for Approximate Nearest Neighbour Search with Arbitrary Distances
Elena Garcia-Morato, Maria Jesus Algar, Cesar Alfaro, Felipe Ortega, Javier Gomez, Javier M. Moguerza
Journal-ref: IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society, vol. 7, pp. 1573-1584, 2026
Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Databases (cs.DB)

Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search has become a central task in modern data-intensive applications, particularly when operating on large-scale, heterogeneous, or high-dimensional datasets. However, many existing ANN methods struggle in such scenarios, either because they rely on metric assumptions or because their indexing strategies are not well suited to distributed environments or to settings with constrained memory resources. This work introduces PDASC (Parametrizable Distributed Approximate Similarity Search with Clustering), a distributed ANN search algorithm whose index design jointly addresses three concerns commonly treated separately in the ANN literature: support for arbitrary dissimilarity functions, native distributed execution, and efficient operation under constrained memory environments, avoiding reliance on specialised hardware accelerators or costly memory resources. PDASC builds a distributed hierarchical index that accommodates non-metric and domain-specific similarities while naturally partitioning indexing and search across multiple computing nodes, with a compact per-node memory footprint. By preserving locally informative neighbourhood structure, the proposed index reduces sensitivity to practical manifestations of the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional spaces. We analyse how the index structural parameters govern the trade-offs among recall, computational cost, and memory usage. Experimental evaluation across multiple benchmark datasets and distance functions shows that PDASC achieves competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs while consistently requiring lower per-node memory compared to state-of-the-art ANN methods.

[781] arXiv:2410.23726 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Risk-Aware Alignment Must Incorporate Reward Uncertainty
Debangshu Banerjee, Kintan Saha, Aditya Gopalan
Comments: Updated Version from Towards Reliable RLHF
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We consider the problem of policy optimization with noisy rewards, where the policy is constrained to be in the neighborhood of a reference this http URL study the risk of the policy optimization process, defined to be the chance of obtaining a policy worse off than the reference policy. In an idealized multivariate Gaussian model for the noisy reward function, we show that the regularizer achieving optimal risk in a suitably local neighborhood of the reference policy is the quadratic norm weighted by the reward covariance matrix. This result is used to develop a new policy optimization algorithm based on regularization via reward variance estimates. Experiments across synthetic bandit models, large language models and reward models show that this algorithm yields more robust alignment outcomes than existing approaches.

[782] arXiv:2411.02650 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Neurophysiological Insights into Multimedia-based Education: A PRISMA-ScR Review of fNIRS in Game-Integrated Learning Systems
Shayla Sharmin, Gael Lucero-Palacios, Behdokht Kiafar, Mohammad Fahim Abrar, Mohammad Al-Ratrout, Aditya Raikwar, Roghayeh Leila Barmaki
Comments: 45 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

Game-integrated learning systems (GILS) are a growing form of multimedia education. Neurophysiological evidence can complement behavioral and learning measures when examining how users interact with these environments. This scoping review follows PRISMA-ScR and synthesizes 20 empirical studies published between 2014 and 2025, identified through searches updated in April 2026, in which functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured task-related cortical hemodynamic responses during GILS use. The review maps learning contexts, multimedia platforms, outcome measures, and methodological approaches across the included studies. Individual studies reported differences in cortical responses across interaction conditions and associations with behavioral or learning outcomes. However, only 10 of the 20 studies assessed learning outcomes, and methodological heterogeneity limits cross-study comparisons. These findings do not establish that specific multimedia platforms cause particular neural or learning outcomes. Future research should prioritize standardized methods, ecologically valid learning settings, and evaluation of the feasibility and educational value of real-time neural adaptation.

[783] arXiv:2502.00892 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A declarative approach to specifying Paxos using three-valued modal fixpoint logic
Murdoch J. Gabbay, Luca Zanolini
Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Logic (math.LO)

We present Three-valued Fixpoint Quorum Logic, or 3muQL for short; a three-valued modal fixed-point logic designed for declaratively specifying and reasoning about distributed algorithms, such as the Paxos consensus algorithm.
Our methodology represents a distributed algorithm as a logical theory, enabling correctness properties to be derived directly within the framework -- or revealing logical errors in the algorithm's design when they exist. 3muQL adopts a declarative approach, specifying the overall logic of computation without prescribing control flow. Notably, message-passing and state-transitions are not explicitly modelled, and notions of 'quorum' are abstracted from concrete thresholds to abstract modal operators. This distinguishes our framework from approaches like TLA+. The logical abstraction emphasises the essence of distributed algorithms, offering a novel perspective on their specification and reasoning.
We define the syntax and semantics of 3muQL, explore its theoretical properties, and demonstrate its applicability through a detailed treatment of the Paxos consensus algorithm. By presenting Paxos as a logical theory and deriving its standard correctness properties, we showcase the framework's capacity to handle non-trivial distributed systems.
We envision 3muQL as a versatile tool for specifying and reasoning about distributed algorithms. The Paxos example highlights the framework's ability to capture intricate details, offering a new lens through which distributed algorithms can be specified, studied, and checked.
The ideas we present are easily implemented, and to demonstrate this we have implemented a freely-available proof-of- concept 3muQL model-checker, as an effective prototyping tool.

[784] arXiv:2502.10295 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Fenchel-Young Generalization of Bayesian Principles
Sophia Sklaviadis, Thomas Moellenhoff, Emtiyaz Khan, Andre Martins, Mario Figueiredo
Comments: Under review
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Conjugate Bayes plays a key role in machine learning, ensuring computationally simple posterior updates. We generalize the variational principle behind this computation by using the Fenchel-Young (FY) inequality, which lets us define a generalized evidence lower bound beyond the KL geometry, and at equality, characterizes new generalized posteriors. A generalized notion of conjugacy follows, defined as closure of prior-potential families that are affine under translation by the loss. We show that such families not only preserve additive canonical updating, but also posterior inference with parameter-dependent supports and tuneably heavy tails. This combination is not feasible with standard conjugate Bayes. We derive a new FY generalization of expectation maximization (EM), which recovers classical and Hard EM, and amortized versions. We show examples, including generalized Bayesian linear regression with closed-form bounded support and heavy-tailed posteriors, and a Gaussian mixture with sparse cluster assignments.

[785] arXiv:2502.13024 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Fragility-aware Classification for Risk Characterization and Robust Learning
Zheng Cui, Daniel Zhuoyu Long, Jin Qi, Chen Yang, Ruohan Zhan
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Classification models play a central role in data-driven decision-making applications such as medical diagnosis, recommendation systems, and risk assessment. Traditional performance metrics, such as accuracy and AUC, quantify classification errors and pairwise ranking performance but do not account for the magnitude of errors, i.e., the risk of confident misjudgments. This limitation is particularly consequential in safety-critical and cost-sensitive settings, where overconfident errors can lead to severe outcomes. To address this issue, we propose the Fragility Index (FI), a novel performance metric that evaluates classifiers from a risk-averse perspective by capturing the tail risk of confident misjudgments. We formulate FI within a robust satisficing (RS) framework to quantify classifier sensitivity under distributional uncertainty. Building on this, we develop a tractable surrogate-based training framework and establish provable bounds connecting training fragility to ranking-error FI. We further derive tractable reformulations for a broad class of loss functions, including cross-entropy, hinge-type, and Lipschitz losses, and identify specific conditions under which these reformulations are exact. We also introduce an FI-induced regularizer for deep neural networks. Empirical results on real-world medical diagnosis tasks demonstrate that FI complements existing metrics by revealing error tail risk not reflected in accuracy or AUC. FI-based models achieve competitive predictive performance while generally attaining lower FI. In the simulated human--AI diagnostic workflow, they also achieve lower average operational costs than empirical risk minimization.

[786] arXiv:2502.20115 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Multi-View Causal Discovery without Non-Gaussianity: Identifiability and Algorithms
Ambroise Heurtebise, Omar Chehab, Pierre Ablin, Alexandre Gramfort, Aapo Hyvärinen
Comments: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Causal discovery is a difficult problem that typically relies on strong assumptions on the data-generating model, such as non-Gaussianity. In practice, many modern applications provide multiple related views of the same system, which has rarely been considered for causal discovery. Here, we leverage this multi-view structure to achieve causal discovery with weak assumptions. We propose a multi-view linear Structural Equation Model (SEM) that extends the well-known framework of non-Gaussian disturbances by alternatively leveraging correlation over views. We prove the identifiability of the model for acyclic SEMs. Subsequently, we propose several multi-view causal discovery algorithms, inspired by single-view algorithms (DirectLiNGAM, PairwiseLiNGAM, and ICA-LiNGAM). The new methods are validated through simulations and applications on neuroimaging data, where they enable the estimation of causal graphs between brain regions.

[787] arXiv:2503.01290 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: ACTIVA: Amortized Causal Effect Estimation via Variational Autoencoders
Andreas Sauter, Saber Salehkaleybar, Frank van Harmelen, Aske Plaat, Erman Acar
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Predicting post-intervention distributions from observational data is central to many scientific and decision-making problems, but remains challenging due to causal ambiguity, restrictive modeling assumptions, and the lack of amortization across tasks. We introduce ACTIVA, a transformer-based conditional variational autoencoder for amortized estimation of full interventional distributions from observational data and intervention queries. ACTIVA learns a conditional latent prior that amortizes causal knowledge across diverse training tasks, so that a new causal model drawn from the training distribution is handled in a single forward pass, without interventional data, a causal graph, or per-task fitting. Beyond the training distribution, only a parametric shift of the simulator is tested. We provide a population-level characterization of ACTIVA's estimand, showing that, under idealized expressivity and infinite samples assumptions, ACTIVA's learning objective targets a simulator-weighted mixture over the interventional distributions of causal models that are observationally compatible with the input. Empirically, on synthetic datasets and biologically realistic gene-expression simulations, ACTIVA substantially outperforms a correlational baseline, reduces spurious non-descendant effects, and achieves competitive performance relative to strong amortized baselines. On a pair of observationally equivalent models sharing a single observational dataset, ACTIVA recovers the predicted mixture, validating the theory in a finite-capacity model. Our results show that ACTIVA is a promising approach for estimating interventional distributions from observational data.

[788] arXiv:2503.02129 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Mathematical Theory of Double Descent as Shrinkage, not Overfitting: Matching Bounds for Path-Regularized Multilayer Neural Networks
Hao Yu
Comments: 54 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Statistics Theory (math.ST)

We give a nonasymptotic generalization theory for multilayer fully connected neural networks trained with path regularization, for general Lipschitz losses and without assuming the loss bounded, the architecture sparse, or any width or depth limit. Approximation error is modelled explicitly, and along the way we settle an open problem of E et al. on approximation rates in generalized Barron spaces. We treat the underparameterized and overparameterized regimes separately, which is what allows the resulting curve to be non-monotone in the width. We then prove lower bounds on the error itself, valid at every target and at every local minimizer, and combine them with the upper bounds into a theorem asserting that the error - not merely our bound on it - descends, rises and descends again as the width grows, with a peak exceeding the final plateau by a factor diverging in the sample size. Having both sides of the bound also identifies what drives the ascent, and it is not overfitting: once the regularization exceeds the dual norm of the noise, which the prescribed schedule does at every width, a slow-rate oracle inequality controls the error with no variance term at all. The rise is instead the shrinkage demanded by the regularization that the underparameterized regime requires, and we show it cannot be removed by any width-independent regularization under which the theory's guarantees hold. This mechanism is a property of the estimator analyzed here; we do not claim it accounts for the double descent reported for unregularized training.

[789] arXiv:2503.22244 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Analysis of On-policy Policy Gradient Methods under the Distribution Mismatch
Weizhen Wang, Xinzhe Zhou, Jianping He, Xiaoming Duan
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Policy gradient methods are among the most successful approaches for solving challenging reinforcement learning problems. Despite their empirical success, many state-of-the-art policy gradient algorithms for discounted problems estimate update directions using a sampling distribution that differs from the discounted state distribution required by the policy gradient theorem. In this work, we analyze the impact of this distribution mismatch on policy gradient methods. Specifically, {for tabular direct and softmax parameterizations, we establish global convergence of objective values under biased updates}. {For tabular softmax policies, we further derive the exact leading-order coefficients of the asymptotic objective errors under biased and normalized exact updates. Their ratio provides an explicit criterion for determining when distribution mismatch accelerates or slows asymptotic convergence.} We then extend the analysis to more general policy parameterizations by deriving explicit bounds on both the state distribution mismatch and the induced normalized policy-gradient mismatch in episodic and continuing MDPs. These mismatches vanish at least linearly as the discount factor approaches one. Under an additional smoothness assumption, we further show that the limit inferior of the squared norm of the normalized exact policy-gradient direction along the biased iterates is bounded by $O((1-\gamma)^2)$ in both settings. Our results provide theoretical insights into the robustness of policy gradient methods to distribution mismatch and shed light on the gap between their theoretical formulations and practical implementations.

[790] arXiv:2504.09488 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Kongzi: A Historical Large Language Model with Fact Enhancement
Jiashu Yang, Ningning Wang, Yian Zhao, Chaoran Feng, Junjia Du, Hao Pang, Miao Yu, Xuxin Cheng
Comments: 22 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables. Revised training and evaluation descriptions; corrected derived evaluation summaries and figures; updated author list
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large Language Models (LLMs) can exhibit factual inaccuracies during long-chain reasoning or under misleading prompts, limiting their reliability in historical analysis. We propose Kongzi, a language model for historical understanding and reasoning that combines continued pre-training on historical corpora, supervised fine-tuning, and fact-enhanced reinforcement learning. Its factuality reward compares entities and relations extracted from generated responses with historical references through knowledge-graph similarity. We evaluate 0.5B and 7B models on historical question answering and counterfactual reasoning, using reported ratings from three LLM judges, and on CMMLU-Chinese-History. Kongzi-7B receives the highest historical-accuracy ratings among the compared models under all three judges. Reinforcement learning improves the mean answer scores of both model sizes and their CMMLU-Chinese-History accuracy, although Kongzi-7B remains below the strongest reported baselines on that benchmark. These descriptive results support further study of factuality rewards for historical language models.

[791] arXiv:2504.20310 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Does More Compute Make Every Adversarial Attack Transferable?
Greg Gluch, Shafi Goldwasser, Anastasiia Struss
Comments: 60 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Transferable attacks, or transferable jailbreaks, are a particularly strong version of adversarial examples that fool all defenders in a class. In this work, we study when more compute enables transferable attacks. We show that, when there is a quadratic gap in computational resources between attacker and defender, every learnable classification task admits either a transferable attack or an adversarial defense. For generative tasks, this dichotomy fails below a quadratic gap, i.e., more compute for the attacker does not lead to a transferable attack.
We prove a stronger result that implies this failure: a defense that spends additional computation after it sees the input can be provably strictly stronger than every defense that publishes a fixed model. This result provides formal evidence that increasing inference-time compute can improve robustness, as empirically observed by Zaremba et al. (2025). We assume the existence of an array of cryptographic primitives: identity-based fully homomorphic encryption, publicly verifiable zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge, non-parallelizing languages, and incrementally verifiable computation.

[792] arXiv:2504.21323 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: How to Backdoor Image Knowledge Distillation
Qian Ma, Chen Wu, Prasenjit Mitra, Sencun Zhu
Comments: Accepted as a regular paper for the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer behavior from a large teacher model to a smaller student. It is often assumed to be safe when the teacher is clean, because classic backdoor attacks rely on poisoned labels and triggers in supervised training, whereas distillation trains the student to match a teacher's outputs. We show that this assumption can fail when the distillation dataset itself is poisoned. Our attack injects triggered and manipulated images that a clean teacher already predicts as an attacker chosen target label, which causes the student to learn a backdoor even though the teacher remains unaffected. We evaluate this threat across multiple manipulation strategies, including targeted adversarial perturbations and targeted GAN based class transitions, and study how distillation settings influence both accuracy and attack success. We show that the attack remains effective even at a 10% poisoning rates. The results demonstrate that a clean teacher alone is not a sufficient safeguard: poisoned distillation data can produce a strongly backdoored student while maintaining competitive performance on clean images. These findings show that the integrity and provenance of distillation data are part of the security boundary of data intensive KD pipelines, even when the teacher itself is trusted.

[793] arXiv:2505.05492 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: DetoxAI: a Python Toolkit for Debiasing Deep Learning Models in Computer Vision
Ignacy Stępka, Lukasz Sztukiewicz, Michał Wiliński, Jerzy Stefanowski
Comments: Published at ECML PKDD 2025, Demo Track
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

While machine learning fairness has made significant progress in recent years, most existing solutions focus on tabular data and are poorly suited for vision-based classification tasks, which rely heavily on deep learning. To bridge this gap, we introduce DetoxAI, an open-source Python library for improving fairness in deep learning vision classifiers through post-hoc debiasing. DetoxAI implements state-of-the-art debiasing algorithms, fairness metrics, and visualization tools. It supports debiasing via interventions in internal representations and includes attribution-based visualization tools and quantitative algorithmic fairness metrics to show how bias is mitigated. This paper presents the motivation, design, and use cases of DetoxAI, demonstrating its tangible value to engineers and researchers.

Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Programming Languages (cs.PL)

Although the $\lambda$I-calculus is a natural fragment of the $\lambda$-calculus, obtained by forbidding the erasure of arguments, its equational theories did not receive much attention. The reason is that all proper denotational models studied in the literature equate all non-normalizable $\lambda$I-terms, whence the associated theory is not very informative. The goal of this paper is to introduce a previously unknown theory of the $\lambda$I-calculus, induced by a notion of evaluation trees that we call "Ohana trees". The Ohana tree of a $\lambda$I-term is an annotated version of its Böhm tree, remembering all free variables that are hidden within its meaningless subtrees, or pushed into infinity along its infinite branches.

We then prove a Commutation Theorem stating that the normal form of the Taylor expansion of a $\lambda$I-term coincides with the Taylor expansion of its Ohana tree. As a corollary, we obtain that the equality induced by Ohana trees is compatible with abstraction and application.
Subsequently, we introduce a denotational model designed to capture the equality induced by Ohana trees. Although presented as a non-idempotent type system, our model is based on a suitably modified version of the relational semantics of the $\lambda$-calculus, which is known to yield proper models of the $\lambda$I-calculus when restricted to non-empty finite multisets. [795] arXiv:2505.11109 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: MAVOS-DD: Multilingual Audio-Video Open-Set Deepfake Detection Benchmark
Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Vlad Hondru, Marius Popescu, Radu Tudor Ionescu, Fahad Shahbaz Khan, Mubarak Shah
Comments: Accepted at IEEE Big Data 2026
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multimedia (cs.MM)

We present the first large-scale open-set benchmark for multilingual audio-video deepfake detection. Our dataset comprises nearly 350 hours of real and fake videos across eight languages, with 59% of data being generated. For each language, the fake videos are generated with several distinct audio and video deepfake generation models, selected based on their quality, via visual inspection. We organize the training, validation and test splits such that only a subset of the chosen generative models and languages are available during training, thus creating several challenging open-set evaluation setups. We perform experiments with various pre-trained and fine-tuned deepfake detectors proposed in recent literature. Our results show that state-of-the-art detectors are not currently able to maintain their performance levels when tested in our open-set scenarios. We publicly release our data and code for non-commercial use at this https URL.

[796] arXiv:2505.18374 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: ShIOEnv: A Command Evaluation Environment for Grammar-Constrained Synthesis and Execution Behavior Modeling
Jarrod Ragsdale, Rajendra Boppana
Comments: 25 pages, 7 figures
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We introduce ShIOEnv, a Gymnasium-compatible Bash environment for synthesizing execution-annotated shell input traces. Datasets containing such traces are useful for training models to perform execution-free shell simulation, which in turn is useful for deploying honeypots for cyber deception. Existing datasets, such as NL2CMD and other Bash command corpora, do not include complete execution artifacts (stdout, stderr, exit status, and changes to the system's state) associated with a command's execution. ShIOEnv synthesizes shell inputs, executes them in a controlled system context, and records stdout, stderr, exit status, and structured filesystem and environment patches. Unconstrained (random) generation of shell inputs (command and arguments) results in multiple instances of arguments that are mostly redundant or result in execution errors. We introduce grammar-constrained synthesis to generate syntactically valid arguments with high input irreducibility, which we estimate through self-ablative contrasts of execution artifacts. We prepare 1.6M samples using grammar-constrained and unconstrained synthesis and collect their execution artifacts for 86 Linux/Bash utilities. Using this dataset, we train small language models (CodeT5) and evaluate their accuracy in predicting the actual execution behavior of attacker-sourced Bash commands. These models outperform commonly used rule-based simulation (Cowrie) and prompted large language models by up to 14.2 pp in output edit similarity (O-ES). We enhance the NL2CMD dataset by constructing 500K samples executable in a grounded system context along with their complete execution artifacts. We empirically demonstrate that models trained on grammar-constrained samples outperform those trained on NL2CMD samples by 22.5 pp in O-ES. ShIOEnv, command grammars, and 2.1M samples used in our primary evaluations are released for use by other researchers.

[797] arXiv:2505.21055 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Agent-Environment Alignment via Automated Interface Generation
